segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated strictly according to the Law of our ancestors, and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prisons,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I even received letters to the brothers in Damascus, and I was traveling there to bring those who were there as well to Jerusalem, bound, to be punished.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As I was on my way and coming near Damascus, about midday a great light from heaven suddenly flashed around me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I came into Damascus led by the hand by those who were with me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: A certain Ananias, a man devout according to the Law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: came to me, stood beside me, and said to me, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight!’ And at that very moment I regained my sight and saw him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He said, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear the voice from his own mouth,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: because you will be a witness for him to all people of what you have seen and heard.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and saw him saying to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I was imprisoning and beating those who believed in you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing there, approving, and guarding the cloaks of those who were killing him.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They listened to him up to this statement; then they raised their voices and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Away from the earth with such a man! It is not right for him to live!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were shouting, throwing off their cloaks, and flinging dust into the air,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks and said he was to be interrogated under the lash, so that he could find out why they were shouting against him like this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they had stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and has not been condemned?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and reported it, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The commander came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The commander answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum of money.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “But I was born a citizen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So those who were about to interrogate him withdrew from him at once, and the commander too was afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he unbound him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and stood him before them.

notes.note: The Greek says literally “the Hebrew dialect.” Many scholars think this means Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea, which Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish from Hebrew. Others hold that Hebrew itself is meant. The text keeps the Greek term and leaves the question open.

notes.traditional: brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel
notes.note: To sit at a teacher’s feet is to be his pupil; Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and teacher of the Law in Jerusalem (Acts 5:34). The punctuation is uncertain: the phrase can go with what precedes, as here, or with what follows (“brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel”). Either way Paul claims a Jerusalem upbringing and a strict training in the Law.
In Acts “the Way” is a name for the movement of Jesus’s followers (for example Acts 9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14). The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or path.
Here “the brothers” are fellow Jews in the synagogues of Damascus, not followers of Jesus. Paul is speaking as a Jew to a Jewish crowd, whom he has just addressed as “brothers and fathers.”
The Greek word can be a polite “sir” or the title “Lord.” Paul does not yet know who is speaking, but he is answering a voice from heaven, so “Lord” is kept, as in most translations.

notes.traditional: heard not the voice; some versions “did not understand the voice”
notes.note: Acts 9:7 says Paul’s companions heard the voice but saw no one. Some translations reconcile the two accounts by rendering this verse “did not understand the voice,” appealing to a difference in Greek case; most grammarians doubt that the distinction holds. The text translates the verb in its ordinary sense and leaves the tension visible.

notes.traditional: receive thy sight ... I looked up upon him
notes.note: The Greek verb means both “look up” and “see again,” and it is used twice here: Ananias’s command and Paul’s response are the same word. The second occurrence, which is followed by “at him,” could also be rendered “I looked up at him.”

notes.traditional: the Just One; the Righteous One
notes.note: A title for the Messiah, used also in Acts 3:14 and 7:52. The Greek adjective covers what English divides among “righteous,” “just” and “innocent.”

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it names the non-Jewish peoples. It is this statement—that the risen Jesus sent Paul away from Jerusalem to non-Jews—that ends the crowd’s willingness to listen.

The Greek title, literally “leader of a thousand,” was the standard Greek equivalent for a Roman military tribune, here the officer commanding the cohort garrisoned in Jerusalem. Many translations use “tribune”; “commander” is used here because the same Greek word also serves for senior officers in general.

notes.traditional: bound him with thongs; stretched him out for the whips
notes.note: The Greek can mean that Paul was stretched out and tied “with the straps,” or stretched out “for the lashes,” that is, for the whipping. The word usually means a leather strap or thong, and a different word is used for the whip in verse 24, so the first reading is followed here. Many translations take the second.

The Greek says simply “a Roman,” which in this context means a holder of Roman citizenship, not someone from Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being flogged without trial, and an officer who violated this could be held to account, which is why the soldiers back away at once.

candidates.reason: Recurs through Acts 21–25 and in the Gospels and Revelation, and translations split between “tribune,” “commander” and “captain.”
Occurs across the Gospels and Acts, and translations vary between “council” and “Sanhedrin,” which a reader could take for two different bodies.
Recurs in the Gospels and Acts, and could be “of Nazareth,” “the Nazarene” or “the Nazorean”; Acts 24:5 uses the plural for the movement, so the choice needs coordinating.
As a name for the Jesus movement in Acts (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22) it needs a uniform rendering and capitalization.
With Ἑβραϊστί in John and Revelation, translations differ between “Hebrew” and “Aramaic,” and the choice should be uniform across books.
